messages.subject: Sum to Zero Constraints for Ridge Regression across Choices
parts:
Dear All, 

Preface- I'm relatively new to INLA; I'm a DPhil student in Sociology with a background in Statistics for Masters & Undergrad. 
My problem is as follows: 

I have survey responses from a vote-choice question; each i = {1,..,N} respondent says they vote for candidate j={1,2,3}. I have a very large number of covariates X (potentially p>n, but forget that for now), and as such I'd like to implement a degree of regularisation; I'd like to do this via Ridge regression. 

I'd like to run a poisson model (equivalent to the multinomial) of the following form: 

# likelihood
Y_i ~ pois(mu_i)
mu_i = exp(eta_i)
eta_i = lambda_i + alpha_j + sum_d[ x_ijd * beta*_jd]

# prior on multinomial equivalency parameter 
lambda_i ~ gamma(0.01,0.01)

# prior on candidate intercept 
alpha_j ~ norm(0,tau_alpha)

# prior on random slopes 
beta_jd ~ norm(0,tau_beta_j)
# sum to zero constraint
beta_jd* = beta_jd - mean(beta_d)


In Inla the closest I've gotten to this is: 

formula = V ~ -1 + f(id.i,  model="iid") +f(idx.j,  model="iid") + f(idx, replicate = idx.j, model="z", Z = X)

model_inla <-inla(formula,
                  family = "poisson",
                  data = model_data,
                  control.family=list(link='log'),
                  control.predictor=list(link=1, compute=TRUE),
                  control.compute = list(config=TRUE))

Where:
V is the stacked 1/0 vote choice vector in long format, of size N*3; 
id.i is the index for the respondent id, or rep(1:N,3);
idx is the index of observations, or 1:(N*3);
idx.j is the index of choices, or rep(1:3,each = N).

What I seem to be missing from the above is a constraint such that the covariate effects by choice can sum to zero. 
I'm aware of the cross function, but I have not been able to implement it - if you could point me to some useful examples, or explain how it would work in this case, I'd be very grateful. 
Please also let me know if I've messed this up entirely.

Many thanks in advance, 
Roberto

Hi,

1) hard to say in general, but often, yes, as long as the posterior is computable (I.e. not entirely unidentifiable, so that the numerical methods don’t collapse) prediction tends to be ok without explicit constraints. Each individual component may have a large posterior variance, but the nearly unidentifiable parts will have strong negative correlation, so that their combined effect can have a small variance.

2) not sure, but probably not one that can be specified in inla, if I understood Håvard’s comment correctly.

Finn

1) if I'm interested merely in prediction, can I safely ignore constraints all-together? is there any gain in predictive power from identifiability beyond being able to make interpretable inference?

2) is there a way in which I could use some structure of priors in order to enforce a behaviour of the coefficients which is similar to the sum-to-zero I'm looking for?

Hi,

Yes, “adjusting” the posterior samples to impose constraints doesn’t produce the same result, unless the adjustment is done in exactly the right way (and that isn’t simple, or necessarily doable).

A valid approach would be to throw away all samples that don’t fulfill the constraint, but that’s clearly impractical! That approach is only useful for some types of inequality constraints.
